title: Exposure therapy for OCD
description: Exposure and response prevention is a behaviour therapy for obsessive-compulsive disorder: people gradually face what triggers their obsessions while resisting the urge to carry out the compulsion, until the anxiety fades on its own. Two studies by the same group measured the brain's energy use before and after treatment. In people who improved, the caudate, part of the striatum, used less energy afterwards. The same was found with the medicine fluoxetine. In this episode brightness stands for energy use (glucose metabolism) relative to the rest of the brain. It shows the change since before treatment: violet means less than before.
caveat: These are two small, older studies by one research group, with 9 people in each behaviour therapy sample, using PET scans of glucose use rather than fMRI. The decrease was found in people who responded to treatment; in the first study it did not change in those who did not respond or in people without OCD, and in the second it was smaller in poor responders. The sources read do not report how the brain differed from people without OCD before treatment, so the first part is drawn at rest. These are averages across groups of people, not a picture of any one person's brain. Treatments help many people, not everyone, and in different ways. This is not medical advice: talk to a doctor or therapist about what is right for you.

phases.name: Before treatment
phases.caption: Before treatment. The comparison here starts from each person's own level, so the brain is drawn at rest.

phases.name: Ten weeks of therapy
phases.caption: About ten weeks of facing triggers without carrying out the compulsion. People were not scanned during this time.

citations.authors: Baxter LR, Schwartz JM, Bergman KS, Szuba MP, Guze BH, Mazziotta JC, Alazraki A, et al.
citations.title: Caudate glucose metabolic rate changes with both drug and behavior therapy for obsessive-compulsive disorder.
citations.quote: We used positron emission tomography to investigate local cerebral metabolic rates for glucose (LCMRG1c) in patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder before and after treatment with either fluoxetine hydrochloride or behavior therapy.

citations.authors: Schwartz JM, Stoessel PW, Baxter LR, Martin KM, Phelps ME
citations.title: Systematic changes in cerebral glucose metabolic rate after successful behavior modification treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder.
citations.quote: Nine patients with obsessive-compulsive disorder were studied with positron emission tomography before and after 10 weeks of structured exposure and response prevention behavioral and cognitive treatment.

phases.name: What changed
phases.caption: In people who improved, the caudate uses less energy than before, on both sides in the second study. Before treatment, activity in the orbitofrontal cortex rose and fell together with the caudate and thalamus across people; after successful treatment, it did so much less.

order.rationale: This last part is a summary of what the studies did not find or did not measure, not a later point in time.

regions.explanation: Used less energy after treatment in people who responded, on the right in one study and on both sides in a second study by the same group. In the first study it did not change in non-responders or people without OCD; in the second it was smaller in poor responders. Brightness stands for glucose use relative to the rest of the brain, not activity measured by fMRI.
